claim.why_it_matters: The two rule sub-clauses are lifted out of the CONVERT function clause and become siblings of '## 15.19 CONVERT function'. The neighbouring function 15.20 COS is transcribed correctly ('### 15.20.3 Argument rule', '### 15.20.4 Returned value rule'), so CONVERT is the outlier and any outline- or citation-resolving tool will mis-parent CONVERT's argument and returned-value rules.

verdict.reasoning: REFUTED as a PDF-vs-markdown discrepancy, though the raw H2/H3 observation is factually true. Three independent findings. (1) NO CONTENT DIFFERS. Rendered p860 at 300 dpi and compared against page-860.md character by character. Both headings are PRESENT, correctly numbered and correctly titled: the PDF prints '15.19.3 Argument rules' and '15.19.4 Returned value rules'; the markdown carries '15.19.3 Argument rules' and '15.19.4 Returned value rules'. All nine argument rules, the embedded NOTE after rule 5, and the single 15.19.4 returned-value rule are transcribed verbatim with no omission, reordering or wording change. The kind label 'missing-heading' is a misnomer: nothing is missing. What differs is only the markdown '#' depth, i.e. transcription formatting metadata that has no counterpart in the PDF at all. (2) THE CLAIM'S PDF EVIDENCE IS SELF-DEFEATING. The claim argues the PDF prints 15.19.3/15.19.4 'in the same bold sub-clause style as 15.19.1 and 15.19.2', implying the typography establishes the level. I rendered p859 to check. It does not. On p859 '15.19 CONVERT function', '15.19.1 General' and '15.19.2 General format' are all set in the IDENTICAL bold face, at the identical point size, at the identical left margin -- the parent clause is typographically indistinguishable from its children. ISO conveys depth here through the dotted clause NUMBER, not through style. So 'same bold style as 15.19.1' is equally true of 15.19 itself and proves nothing about level. And the clause number -- the only thing the PDF actually asserts about hierarchy -- is transcribed correctly. (3) 'CONVERT IS THE OUTLIER' IS FALSE. Swept ISO_COBOL.md: 276 three-level (x.y.z) headings sit at H2 against 508 at H3, so the heading-depth convention is inconsistent in 276 places document-wide. Inside clause 15 the split is 12 at H2 vs 364 at H3, and the H2 set is not CONVERT-specific -- it also contains 15.3.1, 15.3.2, 15.3.3, 15.4.1, 15.5.3, 15.5.4, 15.5.5 and, in exactly the same function-rule shape as CONVERT, 15.67.4, 15.68.4 and 15.69.4 ('Returned value rules'). CONVERT is one member of a systemic transcription artefact, not a singular anomaly, so the claim's central justification for filing it as a p860 finding does not hold. Citation resolution is unaffected: ISO citations resolve by clause number ('15.19.3'), which is intact, and the anchors / are present and correct. No spec meaning changes. Under the rejection criteria (difference is formatting only; difference does not change meaning), this is not a reportable page-860 content discrepancy.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a PDF-vs-markdown content discrepancy. Both headings are present with the correct clause number, correct title, correct anchors, and verbatim rule text; nothing is missing. The only difference is the markdown heading depth (H2 rather than H3), which is an internal-consistency wart in the transcription's own convention -- and a systemic one, affecting 276 three-level headings document-wide (12 within clause 15, including 15.3.1-15.3.3, 15.4.1, 15.5.3-15.5.5, 15.67.4, 15.68.4, 15.69.4), so CONVERT is not the outlier the claim describes. The claim's supporting evidence is also unsound: on p859 the PDF sets '15.19 CONVERT function', '15.19.1 General' and '15.19.2 General format' in one identical bold style at one identical margin, so the printed typography distinguishes no levels whatsoever and cannot establish that 15.19.3/15.19.4 are children. If the H2/H3 inconsistency is worth fixing it belongs in a single document-wide normalization pass over all 276 sites, not as a structural spec-reconciliation finding against page 860.
